answer.short:
Mean: $9.99$ tomatoes per plant; mode: $10$ tomatoes; median: $10$ tomatoes.

Use $\bar{x}=\frac{\sum xf}{\sum f}$; locate the middle observations using $cf$, and find the tomato count with greatest frequency.

inlines.latex: \begin{aligned}\sum f&=700\\\sum xf&=6994\\\bar{x}&=\frac{\sum xf}{\sum f}\\\bar{x}&=\frac{6994}{700}=\frac{3497}{350}\\\bar{x}&\approx9.99\text{ tomatoes per plant}\end{aligned}

There are 700 plants. The median is the average of the 350th and 351st values. The cumulative frequency increases from 270 at 9 tomatoes to 430 at 10 tomatoes, so both middle values are 10. The median is 10 tomatoes.

, therefore it must be normally distributed.” By drawing the frequency polygon, explain why Hana is wrong.

answer.short: The frequency polygon has two peaks, at $11$ and $15$, with a dip at $13$. It is not bell-shaped, so the distribution is not normal.
answer.worked: Plot $(10,3)$, $(11,12)$, $(12,5)$, $(13,4)$, $(14,5)$, $(15,12)$ and $(16,3)$, and join consecutive points with straight lines. blocks.content: Work with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$

content.prompt: A dataset has mean 10 and standard deviation 2.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many standard deviations above the mean is a score of 14?

answer.worked:
$$\frac{14-10}{2}=2$$
The score is 2 standard deviations above the mean.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many standard deviations below the mean is a score of 6?

answer.worked:
$$\frac{10-6}{2}=2$$
The score is 2 standard deviations below the mean.

children.label: c
children.prompt: How many standard deviations above the mean is a score of 13?

answer.worked:
$$\frac{13-10}{2}=1.5$$
The score is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

children.label: d
children.prompt: How many standard deviations below the mean is a score of 9?

answer.worked:
$$\frac{10-9}{2}=0.5$$
The score is 0.5 standard deviations below the mean.

teachingContext.methodNote: Express the distance above or below the mean as a multiple of the standard deviation.

content.prompt: A dataset has mean 50 and standard deviation 5.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A score is 2 standard deviations above the mean. What is the score?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}x&=50+2\times5\\x&=60\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: A score is 1 standard deviation below the mean. What is the score?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}x&=50-1\times5\\x&=45\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: A score is 3 standard deviations below the mean. What is the score?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}x&=50-3\times5\\x&=35\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: A score is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean. What is the score?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}x&=50+1.5\times5\\x&=57.5\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Multiply the number of standard deviations by the standard deviation, then add to or subtract from the mean.

answer.worked: The magnitude of $z=-2$ is 2, and its negative sign indicates below the mean: 2 standard deviations below the mean.
The magnitude of $z=3$ is 3, and its positive sign indicates above the mean: 3 standard deviations above the mean.

The magnitude of $z=1.5$ is 1.5, and its positive sign indicates above the mean: 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

classification.difficultyReason: The z-score formula is supplied with values already substituted, and the student only rearranges 1.5 = 12/σ to get σ = 8. It is easier than p15-q11, where the student must recall the formula, choose the substitution and handle a negative z-score without any set-up.

inlines.text: An assessment task is marked out of 20. The results of the test are shown below.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Calculate the mean and population standard deviation for these scores. Answer correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
There are $16$ scores, with $\sum x=229$ and $\sum x^2=3451$.

$$\begin{align*}\mu&=\frac{229}{16}\\\mu&=14.3125\\\mu&\approx14.3\\\sigma&=\sqrt{\frac{3451}{16}-\left(\frac{229}{16}\right)^2}\\\sigma&\approx3.3\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the z-score of the student who scored the lowest on the test? Answer to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
The lowest score is $8$. Using the unrounded population standard deviation from part a:

$$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\z&=\frac{8-14.3125}{\sqrt{2775}/16}\\z&\approx-1.9\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Lucy was absent for this task, but her mark is usually 1.5 standard deviations above the mean. What mark should her teacher give her as an estimate? Answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Lucy has $z=1.5$. Using the unrounded population statistics:

$$\begin{align*}x&=\mu+z\sigma\\x&=14.3125+1.5\left(\frac{\sqrt{2775}}{16}\right)\\x&\approx19.25\end{align*}$$

Her estimated mark is $19.25$ out of $20$.

inlines.text: An assessment task is marked out of 100. The results of the test are shown below.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Calculate the mean and population standard deviation for these scores. Answer correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
There are $16$ scores, with $\sum x=1217$ and $\sum x^2=93491$.

$$\begin{align*}\mu&=\frac{1217}{16}\\\mu&=76.0625\\\sigma&=\sqrt{\frac{93491}{16}-\left(\frac{1217}{16}\right)^2}\\\sigma&\approx7.594971610\end{align*}$$

To one decimal place, $\mu=76.1$ marks and $\sigma=7.6$ marks. Retain the unrounded values for subsequent calculations.

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the z-score of the student who scored the highest on the test? Answer to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
The highest score is $88$. Using the unrounded statistics from part a:

$$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\z&=\frac{88-76.0625}{\sqrt{93491/16-(1217/16)^2}}\\z&\approx1.571763611\\z&\approx1.6\quad\text{(1 d.p.)}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Mason was absent for this task, but his mark is usually 1.9 standard deviations below the mean. What mark should his teacher give him as an estimate? Answer to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Below the mean gives $z=-1.9$. Using the unrounded statistics from part a:

$$\begin{align*}x&=\mu+z\sigma\\x&=76.0625-1.9\sqrt{93491/16-(1217/16)^2}\\x&\approx61.63205394\\x&\approx61.63\quad\text{(2 d.p.)}\end{align*}$$

The estimated mark is $61.63$ out of $100$.

teachingContext.methodNote: Pages 9–10 relate signed standard deviations to position above or below the mean. Page 11 substitutes into z=(x−μ)/σ; page 12 substitutes into x=μ+zσ. These methods are used for parts b and c.

content.prompt:
A café recorded the number of coffees sold in each hour of a 10-hour trading day.

$12,\ 15,\ 9,\ 14,\ 11,\ 16,\ 13,\ 10,\ 12,\ 8$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Calculate the mean and population standard deviation for these sales. Answer correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
There are $10$ values, with $\sum x=120$ and $\sum x^2=1500$.

$$\begin{align*}\mu&=\frac{120}{10}\\\mu&=12\\\sigma&=\sqrt{\frac{1500}{10}-12^2}\\\sigma&=\sqrt6\\\sigma&\approx2.4\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the z-score of the hour with the highest sales? Answer to 1 d.p.

answer.worked:
The highest value is $16$. Using the unrounded standard deviation from part a:

$$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\z&=\frac{16-12}{\sqrt6}\\z&\approx1.6\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: During a street festival, the sales in one hour were 2.2 standard deviations above the mean. How many coffees were sold in that hour? Answer to 1 decimal place.

answer.worked:
Here $z=2.2$. Using the unrounded statistics:

$$\begin{align*}x&=\mu+z\sigma\\x&=12+2.2\sqrt6\\x&\approx17.4\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Interpret z-score

children.label: a
children.prompt: A student has $z=2$ in their maths test and $z=3$ in their science test. In which test did they perform better relative to the class?

answer.worked: The science score is 3 standard deviations above its class mean, compared with 2 for maths. The higher z-score indicates better performance relative to the class.

children.label: b
children.prompt: A student has $z=-2$ in their maths test and $z=-3$ in their science test. In which test did they perform better relative to the class?

answer.worked: Since $-2>-3$, the maths score has the higher z-score. It is 2 standard deviations below its class mean rather than 3, so the student performed better in maths relative to the class.

children.label: c
children.prompt: For time to swim 50 metres, a student has $z=2$ for freestyle and $z=3$ for butterfly. In which stroke did they perform better relative to the swimmers in that stroke?

answer.short: Freestyle, relative to the swimmers in each stroke.
answer.worked: A lower swimming time is better. The freestyle time is 2 standard deviations above its mean, compared with 3 for butterfly, so freestyle is the better relative performance. The actual times cannot be compared from these z-scores alone.

children.label: d
children.prompt: For time to swim 50 metres, a student has $z=-1$ for freestyle and $z=0$ for butterfly. In which stroke did they perform better relative to the swimmers in that stroke?

answer.short: Freestyle, relative to the swimmers in each stroke.
answer.worked: A lower swimming time is better. The freestyle time is 1 standard deviation below its mean, while the butterfly time equals its mean, so freestyle is the better relative performance. The actual times cannot be compared from these z-scores alone.

teachingContext.methodNote: Compare positions relative to each distribution's mean in standard-deviation units; lower times represent better swimming performance.

content.prompt: Two tests have normally distributed scores. The first test has mean 70 and standard deviation 5. The second test has mean 70 and standard deviation 10.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If someone scored 85, in which test have they performed better relative to the cohort? What would your answer be, without any calculation?

answer.worked: Both means are 70. A score of 85 lies farther above the mean relative to the spread in the first test, so it represents better performance relative to that cohort.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Confirm this by calculating the z-score for each test.

answer.worked:
First test:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\\z&=\frac{85-70}{5}\\z&=3\end{aligned}$$
Second test:
$$\begin{aligned}z&=\frac{85-70}{10}\\z&=1.5\end{aligned}$$
The higher z-score confirms better relative performance in the first test.

inlines.text: If you score 85 in the first test, what would the
score of the same z-score be in the second test?

answer.worked:
The first-test score has $z=3$. For the second test:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\mu+z\sigma\\x&=70+3(10)\\x&=100\end{aligned}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Use the paired curves for the qualitative comparison, calculate z=(x−μ)/σ for each test, and preserve the same z-score to find the equivalent second-test score.

children.prompt: In which test does Tom appear to have performed better?

answer.worked: Looking only at the raw scores, Tom appears to have performed better in Science because $78\%>72\%$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: The mean score for the Science test was 66% and the mean score for the Mathematics test was 62%. Using this information and Tom’s test scores, in which test does he appear to have performed better?

answer.short: Science: 12 percentage points above the mean, compared with 10 percentage points in Mathematics.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Science: }x-\mu&=78-66\\\text{Science: }x-\mu&=12\text{ percentage points}\\\text{Mathematics: }x-\mu&=72-62\\\text{Mathematics: }x-\mu&=10\text{ percentage points}\end{align*}$$
Based on the distances above the means, Tom still appears to have performed better in Science.

children.label: c
children.prompt: The standard deviation of the scores for the Science test was 6% and the standard deviation of the scores for the Mathematics test was 4%. Using all the information you now have, in which test has Tom performed better? Explain your answer.

answer.short: Mathematics: $z_M=2.5$, compared with $z_S=2$. His Mathematics result was further above its mean in standard deviation units.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}z_S&=\frac{x_S-\mu_S}{\sigma_S}\\z_S&=\frac{78-66}{6}\\z_S&=2\\z_M&=\frac{x_M-\mu_M}{\sigma_M}\\z_M&=\frac{72-62}{4}\\z_M&=2.5\end{align*}$$
Tom performed better in Mathematics relative to the group because its z-score is higher. His Mathematics score was 2.5 standard deviations above the mean, compared with 2 in Science. The smaller standard deviation in Mathematics means its scores were more tightly clustered around the mean.

content.prompt:
The marks for five students in the Physics examination are shown.

In the half-yearly the mean was 60 and the standard deviation was 16.

In the yearly examination the mean was 58 and the standard deviation was 12.

inlines.text: Fill in the table, also calculate the change in the z-score. Give z-scores to 2 decimal places where necessary. Calculate each change using the displayed rounded z-scores.

answer.short:
In the order half-yearly z-score, yearly z-score, change:

Olivia: $0.69,\ 0.92,\ +0.23$.

Harriet: $-1.19,\ -1.5,\ -0.31$.

Trinity: $1.5,\ 1.83,\ +0.33$.

Hannah: $-0.56,\ 0.08,\ +0.64$.

Karla: $0.13,\ -0.5,\ -0.63$.
answer.worked:
Use $z_H=\dfrac{x_H-60}{16}$ and $z_Y=\dfrac{x_Y-58}{12}$. Calculate the change as the displayed yearly z-score minus the displayed half-yearly z-score.

Olivia:
$$\begin{aligned}z_H&=\frac{71-60}{16}\\z_H&\approx0.69\\z_Y&=\frac{69-58}{12}\\z_Y&\approx0.92\\\Delta z&=0.92-0.69\\\Delta z&=+0.23\end{aligned}$$
Harriet:
$$\begin{aligned}z_H&=\frac{41-60}{16}\\z_H&\approx-1.19\\z_Y&=\frac{40-58}{12}\\z_Y&=-1.5\\\Delta z&=-1.5-(-1.19)\\\Delta z&=-0.31\end{aligned}$$
Trinity:
$$\begin{aligned}z_H&=\frac{84-60}{16}\\z_H&=1.5\\z_Y&=\frac{80-58}{12}\\z_Y&\approx1.83\\\Delta z&=1.83-1.5\\\Delta z&=+0.33\end{aligned}$$
Hannah:
$$\begin{aligned}z_H&=\frac{51-60}{16}\\z_H&\approx-0.56\\z_Y&=\frac{59-58}{12}\\z_Y&\approx0.08\\\Delta z&=0.08-(-0.56)\\\Delta z&=+0.64\end{aligned}$$
Karla:
$$\begin{aligned}z_H&=\frac{62-60}{16}\\z_H&\approx0.13\\z_Y&=\frac{52-58}{12}\\z_Y&=-0.5\\\Delta z&=-0.5-0.13\\\Delta z&=-0.63\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: With reference to the z-score, which students improved the most?

answer.short: Hannah; her z-score increased the most.
answer.worked: Hannah's z-score increased from $-0.56$ to $0.08$, a change of $+0.64$. This is the greatest increase, so her relative performance improved the most.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Which students performed worse relative to the cohort in the second examination?

answer.worked: Harriet's z-score decreased by $0.31$ and Karla's decreased by $0.63$. Their lower z-scores show worse relative performance in the second examination.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Which student's performance decreased the most?

answer.short: Karla; her z-score decreased the most.
answer.worked: Karla's z-score changed by $-0.63$, compared with Harriet's change of $-0.31$. Karla had the greatest decrease in relative performance.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Which student's performance was the most consistent?

answer.short: Olivia; her z-score changed the least.
answer.worked: The magnitudes of the z-score changes are $0.23$, $0.31$, $0.33$, $0.64$ and $0.63$. Olivia's change has the smallest magnitude, $0.23$, so her relative performance was the most consistent.

content.prompt: For normally distributed scores, use the 68–95–99.7 empirical rule to estimate the percentage of scores with a $z$-score between:

answer.worked:
Using symmetry and the empirical rule:
$$\begin{align*}P(1<Z<2)&\approx\frac{95\%-68\%}{2}\\&=13.5\%\end{align*}$$

Using symmetry and the empirical rule:
$$\begin{align*}P(1<Z<3)&\approx\frac{99.7\%-68\%}{2}\\&=15.85\%\end{align*}$$

Using symmetry and the empirical rule:
$$\begin{align*}P(2<Z<3)&\approx\frac{99.7\%-95\%}{2}\\&=2.35\%\end{align*}$$

Split the interval at the mean:
$$\begin{align*}P(-1<Z<2)&\approx\frac{68\%}{2}+\frac{95\%}{2}\\&=34\%+47.5\%\\&=81.5\%\end{align*}$$

Split the interval at the mean:
$$\begin{align*}P(-1<Z<3)&\approx\frac{68\%}{2}+\frac{99.7\%}{2}\\&=34\%+49.85\%\\&=83.85\%\end{align*}$$

Split the interval at the mean:
$$\begin{align*}P(-2<Z<1)&\approx\frac{95\%}{2}+\frac{68\%}{2}\\&=47.5\%+34\%\\&=81.5\%\end{align*}$$

Split the interval at the mean:
$$\begin{align*}P(-2<Z<3)&\approx\frac{95\%}{2}+\frac{99.7\%}{2}\\&=47.5\%+49.85\%\\&=97.35\%\end{align*}$$

Split the interval at the mean:
$$\begin{align*}P(-3<Z<1)&\approx\frac{99.7\%}{2}+\frac{68\%}{2}\\&=49.85\%+34\%\\&=83.85\%\end{align*}$$

Split the interval at the mean:
$$\begin{align*}P(-3<Z<2)&\approx\frac{99.7\%}{2}+\frac{95\%}{2}\\&=49.85\%+47.5\%\\&=97.35\%\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
On the normal-curve sketch, $8=12-2(2)$ and $16=12+2(2)$, so the interval is within two standard deviations of the mean.

The score 16 days is two standard deviations above the mean. By symmetry, the area above 16 days is approximately
$$\frac{100\%-95\%}{2}=2.5\%.$$

The score 10 days is one standard deviation below the mean. The area below 10 days is approximately
$$\frac{100\%-68\%}{2}=16\%.$$
The expected number of patients is
$$0.16\times400=64.$$
Approximately 64 patients recovered within 10 days.

content.prompt: Each data set is normally distributed.

children.label: a
children.prompt: The standard deviation is 4. If 2.5% of the scores are above 38, find the mean.

answer.worked:
By the empirical rule, 95% of scores lie within two standard deviations of the mean, so 2.5% lie above $\mu+2\sigma$. Thus 38 has $z=2$.
$$\begin{align*}38&=\mu+2(4)\\\mu&=38-8\\\mu&=30\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: The mean is 200. If 0.15% of the scores are below 170, find the standard deviation.

answer.worked:
By the empirical rule, 99.7% of scores lie within three standard deviations of the mean, so 0.15% lie below $\mu-3\sigma$. Thus 170 has $z=-3$.
$$\begin{align*}3\sigma&=200-170\\3\sigma&=30\\\sigma&=10\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: 68% of the scores lie between 41 and 59. Find the mean and the standard deviation.

answer.worked:
By the empirical rule, 68% of scores lie between $\mu-\sigma$ and $\mu+\sigma$.
$$\begin{align*}\mu&=\frac{41+59}{2}\\\mu&=50\\2\sigma&=59-41\\2\sigma&=18\\\sigma&=9\end{align*}$$

answer.short: $z\approx2.33$. Plausible, as it is within 3 standard deviations of the mean.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{19-12}{3}\\&=\frac{7}{3}\\&\approx2.33\end{align*}$$
Since $-3<2.33<3$, the waiting time is within three standard deviations of the mean, so the claim is plausible.

children.label: b
children.prompt: A machine fills bottles with a mean of 600 mL and a standard deviation of 4 mL. The amounts are normally distributed. Tom claims his bottle held 585 mL.

answer.short: $z=-3.75$. Very unlikely, as it is more than 3 standard deviations below the mean.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{585-600}{4}\\&=-3.75\end{align*}$$
Since $-3.75<-3$, the amount is more than three standard deviations below the mean, so the claim is very unlikely.

children.label: c
children.prompt: The heights of students at a school are normally distributed with a mean of 165 cm and a standard deviation of 7 cm. Mia claims there is a student who is 145 cm tall.

answer.short: $z\approx-2.86$. Plausible, as it is within 3 standard deviations of the mean, although it is rare.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{145-165}{7}\\&=\frac{-20}{7}\\&\approx-2.86\end{align*}$$
Since $-3<-2.86<3$, the height is within three standard deviations of the mean, so the claim is plausible, although such a height is rare.

answer.short:
$x = 89.8$ (kg)

Fifteen of the $600$ males is $2.5\%$, which is a $z$-score of $2$ by the empirical rule. Then solve $z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ for $x$.
answer.worked:
Number of male sheep $= \frac{1}{21} \times 12\ 600 = 600$.
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Percentage heavier than } x &= \frac{15}{600} \times 100\% \\
&= 2.5\%
\end{align*}$$
Since $95\%$ of data lies within $2$ standard deviations of the mean, the upper tail beyond $z=2$ is $2.5\%$.
$$\begin{align*}
z &= \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \\
2 &= \frac{x - 76.2}{6.8} \\
x - 76.2 &= 13.6 \\
x &= 89.8
\end{align*}$$
So $x = 89.8 \text{ kg}$.

content.prompt:
The graph shows a normal distribution.
Approximately $99.7\%$ of the area under the curve is bounded by $x = 25$ and $x = 145$.

What are the values of $\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?

$\text{A. }\mu = 60 \text{ and } \operatorname{Var}(X) = 20$
$\text{B. }\mu = 60 \text{ and } \operatorname{Var}(X) = 400$
$\text{C. }\mu = 85 \text{ and } \operatorname{Var}(X) = 20$
$\text{D. }\mu = 85 \text{ and } \operatorname{Var}(X) = 400$

answer.worked:
The bounds are symmetric about the mean.
$$\begin{align*}
\mu &= \frac{25 + 145}{2} \\
&= 85
\end{align*}$$
Since $99.7\%$ of the area is within three standard deviations of the mean:
$$\begin{align*}
3\sigma &= 145 - 85 \\
3\sigma &= 60 \\
\sigma &= 20
\end{align*}$$
Therefore:
$$\begin{align*}

children.prompt:

The following claim is made:

‘Brand A light bulbs are more likely to be defective than Brand B light bulbs.’

Is this claim correct? Justify your answer, with reference to z-scores or standard deviations or the normal distribution.

answer.short: No. For both brands, 400 hours has $z=-2$, so both have the same probability of being defective.
answer.worked:
For Brand A:

content.prompt: The weights of 10 000 newborn babies in NSW are normally distributed. These weights have a mean of 3.1 kg and a standard deviation of 0.35 kg. How many of these newborn babies have a weight between 2.75 kg and 4.15 kg?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}z_{2.75}&=\frac{2.75-3.1}{0.35}=-1\\z_{4.15}&=\frac{4.15-3.1}{0.35}=3\end{align*}$$
Using the empirical rule and symmetry,
$$\begin{align*}P(-1<Z<3)&\approx0.34+0.4985\\&=0.8385\\f&\approx10\,000\times0.8385\\&=8385.\end{align*}$$
Approximately 8385 babies.

content.prompt:
A set of scores is normally distributed.
A score of $12$ has a z-score of $-2$ while a score of $21$ has a z-score of $+1$.
Calculate the mean of the scores.

answer.worked:
The difference in standard deviations between the two scores is:
$$\begin{align*}
1 - (-2) &= 3 \text{ standard deviations}
\end{align*}$$
The difference in the raw scores is:
$$\begin{align*}
21 - 12 &= 9
\end{align*}$$
Therefore, one standard deviation $\sigma$ is:
$$\begin{align*}
\sigma &= \frac{9}{3} \\
&= 3
\end{align*}$$
Using the z-score formula $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ for the score of $21$:
$$\begin{align*}
1 &= \frac{21 - \mu}{3} \\
3 &= 21 - \mu \\
\mu &= 21 - 3 \\
\mu &= 18
\end{align*}$$
The mean is $18$.

Worked example: A normal distribution has a mean of 120. If 16% of the scores are below 108, find the standard deviation.
By the empirical rule, 68% of scores lie within one standard deviation of the mean, so 32% lie outside it. By symmetry, 16% lie below $\mu-\sigma$.

Thus 108 has $z=-1$.
$$\begin{align*}-1&=\frac{108-120}{\sigma}\\-1&=\frac{-12}{\sigma}\\\sigma&=12\end{align*}$$

[Pedagogy audit v2 · New teaching] Add a short worked example that finds the z-score of a claimed value and compares it with the 3σ limit to judge whether it is plausible.
Worked example: The mass of a loaf of bread is normally distributed with a mean of 650 g and a standard deviation of 12 g. A customer claims a loaf had a mass of 700 g. Is the claim plausible? Why?
$$\begin{align*}z&=\frac{700-650}{12}\\&=\frac{25}{6}\\&\approx4.17\end{align*}$$
By the empirical rule, approximately 99.7% of values have a $z$-score between $-3$ and $3$.

Since $4.17>3$, a mass of 700 g is more than three standard deviations above the mean, so the claim is very unlikely.
Guided practice:
Proposed question: Is each claim plausible? Why?
a) The waiting time for a bus is normally distributed with a mean of 12 minutes and a standard deviation of 3 minutes. Aisha claims she waited 19 minutes.
b) A machine fills bottles with a mean of 600 mL and a standard deviation of 4 mL. The amounts are normally distributed. Tom claims his bottle held 585 mL.
c) The heights of students at a school are normally distributed with a mean of 165 cm and a standard deviation of 7 cm. Mia claims there is a student who is 145 cm tall.
Answers: a) $z\approx2.33$. Plausible, as it is within 3 standard deviations of the mean.; b) $z=-3.75$. Very unlikely, as it is more than 3 standard deviations below the mean.; c) $z\approx-2.86$. Plausible, as it is within 3 standard deviations of the mean, although it is rare.

entries.description:
Ordered syllabus bullet list:
1. Identify the normal distribution as a continuous probability distribution that is used to model many naturally occurring phenomena
2. Identify the graph of the probability density function of a normal distribution, the normal curve, as an ‘ideal’ bell-shaped curve, symmetrical about its mean which is equal to its mode and median, and as having most values concentrated about the mean
3. Identify contexts that can be approximately modelled by a normal random variable
4. Use the notation X ∼ N(μ, σ²) to represent a normally distributed random variable that has mean μ and standard deviation σ
5. Represent probabilities associated with the normal distribution by areas of shaded regions under the normal curve, which may extend to ±∞
6. Apply the empirical rule to make judgements and solve problems involving probabilities of normally distributed data: that for normal distributions, approximately 68% of data lie within one standard deviation of the mean, approximately 95% within two standard deviations of the mean and approximately 99.7% within three standard deviations of the mean
7. Use graphing applications to explore the normal distribution, graph the probability density function f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))]e^{−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)}, verify the empirical rule and graph the cumulative distribution function
8. Recognise features of the normal curve, and identify the global maximum and points of inflection
9. Distinguish between a standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and the non-standard normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ
10. Define the z-score, or standardised score, by the formula z = (x−μ)/σ, where μ is the mean and σ is the standard deviation, and x is an observed value of a random variable
11. Interpret the z-score as the number of standard deviations a score lies above or below the mean
12. Use z-scores to compare scores from different sets of data and justify conclusions
13. Use z-scores to identify probabilities of events less or more extreme than a given outcome and solve problems using tables for the standard normal distribution
14. Solve problems involving finding the mean or standard deviation of a normal random variable given the probability of an event less or more extreme than a given outcome
15. Use z-scores to make judgements related to probabilities of certain events or given sets of data assuming an underlying normal distribution

entries.description: Properties of the Normal Distribution

The normal distribution is a special continuous probability distribution.
A normal distribution is bell-shaped and symmetric about its mean.
The mean, median, and mode are all equal.

entries.description:
Finding the Equivalent Score
For a score in dataset A, to find the equivalent score in dataset B:
1. Calculate z-score of the raw score in dataset A. z_A = (x_A − μ_A)/σ_A
2. Calculate the raw score in dataset B using dataset A’s z-score. x_B = μ_B + z_Aσ_B

presentation.workingLayout: Two columns separated by a thin vertical rule; calculate the mathematics z-score on the left, then the equivalent English score on the right.

entries.description:
Left column:
1. Calculate z-score for maths
z_M = (x_M − μ_M)/σ_M
z_M = (64 − 59)/9
     = 0.56

Right column:
2. Calculate equivalent score in English using maths z-score
x_E = μ_E + z_Mσ_E
     = 50 + 0.56(6)
     = 53.36

entries.description:
We want P(Z ≤ z) = 0.001
This would be a negative z-score, so
P(Z ≤ −z) = P(Z ≥ z)
             = 1 − P(Z ≤ z)
             = 1 − 0.001
             = 0.999
Using the table, P(Z ≤ 3.1) = 0.999
So z = −3.1:
−3.1 = (100 − μ)/2
−6.2 = 100 − μ
μ = 106.2 g

entries.description: PDF for Standard Normal Curve

For any normal curve with μ and σ:
 f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))] · e^{−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)}

For the standard normal curve μ = 0, σ = 1:
 φ(z) = [1/√(2π)]e^{−(1/2)z²}
Notice that every normal curve is a transformation of the standard curve f(x) = φ((x−μ)/σ)

entries.description:
The standard curve φ(z) has these properties:
• Total area under the curve is 1.
• Even symmetry.
• Mean, median, mode (global max) at z = 0.
• y-intercept at 1/√(2π) ≈ 0.4.
• y → 0 as z → ±∞
• Points of inflection are 1 SD from the mean.
